**Calibration changes confidence while trying to preserve useful discrimination.** Platt scaling fits a sigmoid with learned slope and intercept to binary scores. Temperature scaling fits one positive scalar T to multiclass logits using a held-out calibration set. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)

With logits (2,1,0), T=1 gives approximate probabilities (0.665,0.245,0.090). T=2 yields roughly (0.506,0.307,0.186): the distribution is softer, but class one still has the largest probability. Dividing every logit by the same positive number preserves their order, and softmax preserves that order too.

**Therefore top-one predictions remain unchanged**, apart from numerical or tie-handling details. A smaller temperature sharpens confidence; a larger one increases uncertainty. This can improve probability quality without correcting any mistaken class ranking.

One scalar cannot repair arbitrary class-specific errors or distribution shift. Platt scaling is originally binary, so a multiclass use requires an explicit extension. Fit calibration separately from model training and final evaluation, then monitor it under the deployment distribution. A calibration transform is a probability adjustment, not a substitute for a better classifier.

**Technical details and references.**

Platt scaling fits a sigmoid with slope/intercept to a binary score; multiclass extensions require a specified construction. Temperature scaling fits a single positive scalar on held-out multiclass logits. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)

$$p_i(T)=\frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}},\qquad T>0.$$

Dividing all logits by the same positive value preserves their ordering, so top-1 class predictions remain unchanged aside from numerical/tie effects. Larger temperature softens probabilities; smaller temperature sharpens them. It cannot fix misranked classes or arbitrary class-specific calibration errors. Fit on independent calibration data and recheck under distribution shift.
